match.reason: The bank point explains the general purposes of punishment, while the new point asks students to match fines, community correction orders and imprisonment to those purposes, so it is a related but different idea.

draft.title: Sanctions and their purposes
card: Fine
A sum of money the offender must pay. It punishes and can deter, and it suits less serious offences. It does little to rehabilitate.
Community correction order

A CCO lets the offender stay in the community under conditions set by the court, such as unpaid work, treatment or supervision. It can rehabilitate and punish while the offender stays connected to family and work.
Imprisonment
The offender is held in custody. It punishes, denounces the crime and protects the community while the offender is held. It can also deter, but time in prison may make rehabilitation harder.
A court chooses the sanction that best fits the purposes it wants to achieve in the case in front of it.
draft.remember: Each sanction fits some purposes better than others, so the court matches the sanction to the purposes it needs.

a.q: Which sanction is best suited to protecting the community from an offender who is a danger to others?
opts: Imprisonment
A fine
A community correction order
A good behaviour bond
a.why: Imprisonment removes the offender from the community while they are held, so it protects others in that time. A fine leaves the offender free, so it does little to protect the community from a dangerous person.
a.clue: Which sanction keeps the offender away from the public?

b.q: Dani, a first-time offender in Geelong, stole from her employer after losing her job. A judge wants her to repay the harm and get help with gambling, while she keeps her new job. Which sanction best fits?
opts: A CCO with unpaid work and treatment conditions
A short term of imprisonment
A fine only
Imprisonment, to denounce the crime
b.why: A CCO can include unpaid work and treatment, which punish and help rehabilitate, while Dani stays in her job. A fine only would do little to address the gambling, and imprisonment would remove her from work.
b.clue: Which sanction allows conditions such as treatment while she stays in the community?

b.best: A CCO with unpaid work and treatment conditions

problems.detail: The scenario is confusing. Dani 'stole from her employer after losing her job' yet 'keeps her new job', so it is unclear whose employer she stole from, or when.

The right option is the only one with precise detail ('with unpaid work and treatment conditions'), and it echoes the stem ('repay the harm', 'get help with gambling'). A student could pick it without knowing what a CCO does.
'Repay the harm' is loose. It could suggest a fine or compensation rather than unpaid work, which repays the community rather than the employer.
'A good behaviour bond' is not the current Victorian term; Victoria uses adjourned undertakings. It is only a distractor, but it uses outdated terminology for Victorian students.

a.q: Which purpose does imprisonment serve better than a fine or a CCO?
opts: Protecting the community while the offender is held
Rehabilitating the offender through treatment
Keeping the offender connected to family and work
Suiting offences that are less serious
a.why: Imprisonment holds the offender in custody, so others are protected for that time. Rehabilitation through treatment and staying connected to family and work are strengths of a CCO, and prison may make rehabilitation harder.
a.clue: Which sanction removes the offender from the public?

b.q: Dani, 24, has no prior convictions. She stole from the café where she works to pay gambling debts, and the café has kept her on. The judge wants a sanction that punishes her and helps her change, while she keeps working. Which sanction best fits?
opts: A CCO with unpaid work and treatment conditions
A fine set at the value of what she stole
A short prison term to punish and deter her
A long prison term to denounce the crime
b.why: A CCO can punish through unpaid work and help rehabilitate through treatment, while Dani stays in her job. A fine punishes but does little to rehabilitate, so it would not address her gambling. Either prison term would take her away from work.
b.clue: Which sanction can punish and rehabilitate while she stays in the community?
